readerTitle: Two launches beat the plan. Only one learned anything.
caseNote: 가상 사례 두 개 비교 (접이식 물류 상자 제조사, 배송 기사용 경로 앱) + 가상 적용 (베이커리 체인) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 출시는 결과가 아니라 시험의 시작이다. 출시 전에 알아낼 질문과 확인할 행동을 정해 두고 첫 고객 가까이 가야 배운다.
misconception: 출시 후 판매나 가입 숫자가 목표를 넘으면 잘된 것이고, 데이터가 많을수록 더 많이 배운다.

sources.text: Blank, S. (2005). The Four Steps to the Epiphany. 고객 개발(직접 고객을 만나 가설을 검증하는 방식)의 일반 개념
모든 수치와 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 회사와 수치는 설명용 가상입니다. 앱 차트: 가입 2,000명, 첫 경로 계획 1,300명, 일주일 안에 두 번째 경로 계획 400명. 400 ÷ 2,000 = 20%로 카드 문구와 일치합니다.
상자 제조사: 목표 대비 주문 30% 초과, 첫 구매자 25곳 통화, 창고 5곳 방문은 가상 수치입니다. 차트나 계산에 쓰이지 않습니다.
Blank(2005)는 일반 개념의 배경 출처로만 적었고 카드에 인용이나 수치는 없습니다. 게시 전 서지 정보를 확인하세요.

cards.title: Two launches beat the plan. Only one learned anything.
body: A small manufacturer launches a folding plastic crate for warehouses. A software team launches a route-planning app for delivery drivers. Same month.
Both beat their first-month targets. Three months later, one knows exactly what to fix and who to sell to next. The other is still guessing.

image.label: Split scene: folding crates in a warehouse and a route map on a phone
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽은 창고 선반에 쌓인 접이식 플라스틱 상자, 오른쪽은 배송 기사 손에 든 휴대폰 속 경로 지도. 양쪽 위에 똑같이 위로 꺾인 작은 그래프. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You make the crate. Orders are 30% above plan.
body: Your new folding crate sells through three distributors. First-month orders beat your forecast by 30%.
You have the cash and time for one move this month. What do you do first?

options.text: Order a bigger production run before stock runs out
options.feedback: You avoid running out, but you scale whatever is in the product now, including flaws you haven't seen. If buyers don't reorder, you're sitting on crates.

options.text: Call the first buyers and visit a few warehouses to see the crates in use
options.feedback: You give up a few weeks of speed. In return you learn why it sells and whether it will sell again.

options.text: Ask distributors for a monthly sales report by region
options.feedback: Cheap and easy. You'll learn where it sells, but not how it's used or why someone might stop ordering.

cards.title: What the crate maker found by looking.
body: The founder called 25 of the first buyers and visited five warehouses. Two surprises came up.
Most customers used the crates for **returns**, not outbound shipping. And the hinge cracked when forklifts stacked crates six high.
Neither fact showed up in the order numbers. Within weeks, the company had a stronger hinge and a new pitch aimed at retailers with lots of returns.

image.label: A cracked crate hinge next to a returns shelf
image.brief: 창고 장면. 앞쪽에 경첩에 금이 간 접이식 상자 클로즈업, 뒤쪽에는 "Returns"라고 적힌 선반에 상자가 가득. 클립보드를 든 창업자가 메모하는 모습. 실제 브랜드 표시 없음.

cards.title: What the app team saw, and missed.
body: The app team had dashboards with dozens of numbers. They celebrated 2,000 sign-ups in month one.
But nobody had decided in advance which number mattered. Only 20% of drivers came back to plan a second route. No one noticed for two months.

rows.label: Planned a second route within a week

cards.title: Learning after launch
body: **Learning after launch** means treating the first weeks after a launch as a planned period of finding out what's true, then changing course based on it.
A launch tests guesses about who buys, how they use it and whether they come back. Sales numbers answer the first guess. The other two usually need a closer look.
The crate maker had less data than the app team but learned more. It went looking for specific answers.

image.label: Two paths: a pile of numbers versus a few clear questions
image.brief: 두 갈래 길 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 길에는 숫자와 그래프가 어지럽게 쌓여 있고 물음표가 떠 있음. 오른쪽 길에는 "Who buys?", "How do they use it?", "Do they come back?" 세 개의 표지판이 있고 끝에 "Change course" 깃발.

cards.title: Set it up before launch day.
body: The learning starts before anything ships. Four steps:
list: **Write down 2–3 guesses** that matter most, such as who will buy and how they'll use it
**Pick a behavior** that would prove each one: a reorder, a second use, a referral
**Keep a direct line** to your first customers, even if you sell through others
**Set a review date** and decide now what result would make you change course
cards.callout: Data you never asked a question of rarely teaches you anything.

cards.title: Early customers aren't everyone.
body: Your first buyers are often keener and more forgiving than the customers who come later. What delights them may not win the next group.
Small numbers also mislead. One loud complaint can look like a trend.
And learning only helps if you can still act on it. If you've already locked in tooling or a big ad contract, the lessons may arrive too late to use.

cards.title: Now it's a bakery.
body: A bakery chain adds a new sandwich line in three of its shops. You're in charge of the first month.
What do you set up?

options.text: Track daily sandwich sales and compare them to the plan
options.feedback: Easy and useful. It shows whether the launch buzz holds, but not whether the same people come back or why others skip it.

options.text: Have staff note repeat buyers and comments, set a repeat-purchase target, and review on day 30 with a decision agreed in advance
options.feedback: It costs a little staff time. In return you get an answer you can act on, not just a number to watch.

options.text: Run a big discount week to build volume fast
options.feedback: You'll get big numbers, but they mostly measure the discount. It becomes harder to tell who would pay full price.

cards.title: A launch is the start of the test, not the result.
body: Before you launch, decide what you need to find out and how you'll see it. Then get close enough to your first customers to watch.
**Try it today:** for your next launch, even a small one, write down one guess, the behavior that would prove it, and the date you'll check.
